what_was_wrong: The adverbial tag 'tonight' was glued onto the bare host 'I've done'. 'I've done' is a transitive fragment awaiting an object; adding a time adverb without an object yields ungrammatical English ('I've done tonight'). The Marathi 'किती केलंय रात्री' ('how much has been done, at night') is correspondingly incoherent.
prereq_evidence: I've = S38; done = S89; a = S6; lot = S89 (the exact chunk 'I've done a lot' is the core of seed S89 'I think that I've done a lot in a short time', and is already drilled as a phrase at S89). All <= 245.
marathi_basis: IN-COURSE: seed S89 known_text is 'मला वाटतं की मी थोड्या वेळात खूप काही केलंय.' — my replacement is the verbatim substring 'मी खूप काही केलंय'. NOTE the S89 *phrase-level* rendering is 'मला बरंच काही केलंय' with dative मला, which is wrong for a transitive perfect; Marathi marks 1st/2nd person perfective subjects nominative (मी), no ergative. Confirmed: https://sdml.ac.in/blog-Ergative1 and https://talkpal.ai/culture/how-do-you-use-the-ergative-case-in-marathi-past-tense/ . I therefore used the seed-level (correct) मी form, not the phrase-level मला form.
notes: TRADE-OFF FOR THE PARENT: the *incorrect* Marathi 'मला बरंच काही केलंय' DOES already have a known clip in this course (from S89). Choosing it would make this row cost zero clips, but would import a case error. I chose correctness; this costs 1 new known clip. English side re-links free (target1+target2 already exist). Separately: the S89 slot itself carries the मला error — out of my scope, flagged for someone else.

what_was_wrong: 'very well' is a manner adverbial and cannot modify the predicate nominal 'complete rubbish'. 'complete rubbish very well' is not English. The Marathi 'टाकाऊ होता खूप नीट' is the same nonsense ('was rubbish very properly').
prereq_evidence: the = S10; film = S221; was = S42; complete = S248 (this seed); rubbish = S248 (this seed). All <= 248.
marathi_basis: IN-COURSE, VERBATIM: seed S248 known_text is 'मला वाटलं तो सिनेमा अगदी टाकाऊ होता आणि मला माझे पैसे परत हवे आहेत.' — my replacement 'तो सिनेमा टाकाऊ होता' is a substring of it (minus the intensifier अगदी, which the LEGO card also drops). GENDER: सिनेमा is masculine, so तो / होता; this agreement is baked into the LEGO card's होता and my replacement preserves it. Contrast S247 'ते पुस्तक बऱ्यापैकी चांगलं होतं' (neuter पुस्तक → ते/होतं) — the course itself demonstrates it gets this agreement right.
notes: I deliberately chose 'the film was complete rubbish' over 'it was complete rubbish'. Both are grammatical, but 'it' has no antecedent in a standalone drill fragment and would force me to CHOOSE a Marathi gender (तो vs ते) with no evidence; naming सिनेमा makes the masculine agreement evidenced rather than guessed. This does re-use L2's 'the film was' material inside an L1 slot, but that is already the norm here — all four of this LEGO's existing USE phrases open with 'I thought the film was'. Costs 1 known + 2 target clips.

what_was_wrong: Same 'very well' glue on a predicate nominal. Additionally the old Marathi was a concatenation of two LEGO cards with duplicated होता ('सिनेमा खराब होता टाकाऊ होता') — not a sentence. A USE phrase must be a natural complete utterance and this was neither natural nor complete.
prereq_evidence: we = S18; thought = S124; the = S10; film = S221; was = S42; complete = S248; rubbish = S248. All <= 248.
marathi_basis: IN-COURSE for the frame: 'मला वाटलं' attested at S124, S247, S248 (this seed), S374, S387, S615; 'तो सिनेमा ... टाकाऊ होता' verbatim in the S248 seed; 'आम्हाला' attested at S521. The only step not directly attested in-course is the 1pl dative experiencer 'आम्हाला वाटलं'. GROUNDED ONLINE: वाटणे is a dative-subject (experiencer) predicate in Marathi, so the subject takes -ला — आम्ही + -ला = आम्हाला; the verb stays neuter वाटलं. See https://sdml.ac.in/pdfs/semantic-mapping-of-dative-marathi.pdf and https://ling.sprachwiss.uni-konstanz.de/pages/home/butt/main/papers/nijmegen-hnd.pdf .

Because that already exists as S0248L02U01, and '...again' (S0248L01U01), '...in English' (L02U02), '...already' (L02U03), '...yet' (L02B02) and '...today' (L02B04) are all taken too. Switching the subject to 'we' was the shortest route to a non-duplicate, same-register, same-length natural utterance that still drills 'complete rubbish'. MEDIUM not HIGH purely because 'आम्हाला वाटलं' is reference-grounded rather than course-attested — a Marathi speaker glancing at it would settle it in a second. Costs 1 known + 2 target clips.

what_was_wrong: 'very well' glued onto a bare prepositional phrase. 'for your father very well' is not English. The Marathi was the card plus 'खूप नीट' with no verb to modify.
prereq_evidence: to = S1; wait = S82; for = S38; your = S83; father = S240. All <= 269.
marathi_basis: IN-COURSE: 'तुमच्या वडिलांची वाट' is verbatim from this seed's own known_text (S269: 'तुम्हाला तुमच्या वडिलांची वाट का पाहायची नाही?') and from S0269L02U01-U04. The replacement is the composition of those two attested chunks.
notes: NOTE ON THE LEGO CARD: this card's Marathi 'वडिलांची वाट' literally means 'father's wait', i.e. it already contains the verb 'wait' that the English card ('for your father') does not. That is why every tag glued to it produced nonsense. Making the English an infinitive phrase brings the two sides back into alignment while still drilling 'for your father'. I rejected an imperative ('wait for your father') because this course contains NO imperatives — its register is entirely 1st/2nd-person statements and questions. Costs 1 known + 2 target clips.

what_was_wrong: 'to wait very well' is a manner reading nobody intends, and the Marathi 'पाहायची नाही खूप नीट' is not a phrase at all. Worse, the card's Marathi 'पाहायची नाही' carries the NEGATION while the English card 'to wait' does not — so the old row's two sides did not mean the same thing even before the tag was added.
prereq_evidence: I = S1; don't = S19; want = S1; to = S1; wait = S82. All <= 269.
marathi_basis: IN-COURSE, VERBATIM MINUS ONE CHUNK: S0269L02U02 is 'I don't want to wait for your father' = 'मला तुमच्या वडिलांची वाट पाहायची नाही'. Removing 'तुमच्या वडिलांची' leaves exactly 'मला वाट पाहायची नाही'. वाट पाहणे is the compound verb 'to wait', so वाट must stay when the object is dropped.
notes: This replacement deliberately RESTORES the negation baked into the LEGO card's Marathi (नाही) by putting it into the English too, which the old row failed to do. Slightly longer than the old 4-word fragment (5 words) but still a short drill unit and now a well-formed clause. Costs 1 known + 2 target clips.

what_was_wrong: 'why don't you want?' is ungrammatical — 'want' here is a control verb and needs either an object or a stranded 'to'. The Marathi 'तुम्हाला का नाही?' has no predicate at all ('why not to you?').
prereq_evidence: why = S21; don't = S19; you = S1; want = S1; to = S1. All <= 269.
marathi_basis: IN-COURSE: 'मला ते नको आहे' = 'I don't want it' (seed S269-independent, S473) and LEGO S500 L4 'तुम्हाला नको आहे का' = 'don't you want to' — the latter is the same frame with the same 2nd-person dative तुम्हाला, differing only in question word. Substituting का-as-'why' for का-as-yes/no yields 'तुम्हाला का नको आहे?'. ONLINE CORROBORATION that नको आहे = 'don't want' with a dative experiencer: https://polyglotclub.com/wiki/Language/Marathi/Grammar/Negation and https://www.khandbahale.com/language/marathi-dictionary-translation-meaning-of-don%E2%80%99t%20want .
notes: EXPLICIT GAP: the two in-course attestations (S473, S500) sit at seed numbers ABOVE 269. Since Marathi is the learner's native language and the known side is only a comprehension prompt, I treated them as grammatical evidence rather than as vocabulary the learner must have met; if the parent applies strict known-side prerequisite discipline, this item should be re-cut. Also, English 'to?' is stranded and has no Marathi counterpart, so the Marathi reads 'why don't you want (it)?' — a small mismatch a Marathi speaker might want to close by adding a verb. Costs 1 known + 2 target clips.
